facts.claim: Trauma and Recovery: The Aftermath of Violence (Basic Books, 1992) by Judith Lewis Herman, psychiatrist.

Herman describes three stages of recovery. Stage one: establishing safety. Stage two: remembrance and mourning. Stage three: reconnection with ordinary life. 'The first task of recovery is to establish the survivor's safety. This task takes precedence over all others.'

'The first principle of recovery is empowerment of the survivor. She must be the author and arbiter of her own recovery.' Others can give 'advice, support, assistance, affection, and care, but not cure.' Interventions that take control from the survivor can harm recovery even when they seem in her interest.
'Recovery can take place only within the context of relationships; it cannot occur in isolation.' Trauma isolates; a group re-creates a sense of belonging and bears witness.

In the second stage the survivor tells the story 'completely, in depth and in detail'; this work of reconstruction 'actually transforms the traumatic memory'. The therapist is witness and ally, 'in whose presence the survivor can speak of the unspeakable'.
Approaching traumatic memories 'too precipitately leads to a fruitless and damaging reliving of the trauma'; the survivor chooses when to confront them.

Herman, drawing on Pierre Janet, describes traumatic memories as frozen and wordless; they 'lack verbal narrative and context' and are encoded as vivid sensations and images (pp. 37-38 per a course handout). Normal memory works like telling a story that joins the person's life narrative.
Reconstructing the memory in words lets it be integrated into the survivor's life story (Herman citing Janet).

Opening of the book: 'The ordinary response to atrocities is to banish them from consciousness.' 'Atrocities, however, refuse to be buried.' The conflict between the will to deny horrible events and the will to proclaim them aloud is the central dialectic of psychological trauma.
Herman's history chapter treats hysteria, shell shock and domestic violence as the three major paradigms of trauma study of the past hundred years.

Late 1800s Paris: Charcot recorded hysteria symptoms in women and was not interested in their thoughts or in curing them. His followers Janet and Freud talked with patients and concluded hysteria was caused by psychological trauma.

Freud's 1896 paper 'The Aetiology of Hysteria' named premature sexual experience (child abuse) as the root; he later repudiated this view, since so many patients would have meant abuse was more widespread than society would accept.
The 'political context' can support or hinder the study of trauma; domestic abuse and rape were largely unexplored before the 1970s.
